title: Avoiding lethal mutations – How schools can keep research alive and effective
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes introduces the concept of 'lethal mutation', a term coined by Ed Haertel and used by Brown and Campione, to describe how research-based practices lose their potency when oversimplified or misapplied during school implementation. She distinguishes lethal mutations - sound research distorted in practice - from edu-myths, which are wrong from the start, using the analogy that mutations play 'the right notes... in the wrong order'. She traces how three-way differentiation and retrieval-as-daily-quiz became widely adopted mutations of good research, citing a survey by Gareth Bates and James Shea finding 85% of teachers used only short-answer quizzes for retrieval with limited reteaching or corrective feedback. Her three proposed remedies - CPD that builds understanding rather than compliance, communities of practice with room for challenge, and coaching that surfaces mental models rather than just behaviours - reappear as recurring themes across her broader body of work.
points: Hughes's core distinction between edu-myths ('wrong from the start') and lethal mutations ('right in theory but wrong in practice') gives school leaders a precise vocabulary for diagnosing why good research fails in implementation.

She cites survey data (Bates and Shea) showing 85% of teachers use only short-answer quizzes for retrieval practice, with limited reteaching, evidencing how a well-evidenced technique narrows into shallow routine at scale.

Her account of being told early in her career she needed 'three levels of differentiation' to achieve an Outstanding grade illustrates how policy-driven mutations can become embedded orthodoxy long after the evidence has moved on.

Her three proposed remedies (understanding-focused CPD, communities of practice, coaching that surfaces mental models) connect diagnosis to concrete organisational response rather than leaving the problem unresolved.
quotes: This phenomenon is known as the lethal mutation, a term originally coined by Ed Haertel and highlighted in the work of Brown and Campione. It describes how research-based strategies can lose their potency when oversimplified, misunderstood or applied without context.
Unlike edu-myths - which are just wrong from the start - lethal mutations are more dangerous because they begin with good intentions and sound research.
It's a bit like that famous Morecambe and Wise sketch - teachers are playing the right notes, but they're in the wrong order.

While 100% of surveyed teachers reported using retrieval practice regularly, the most common format was short-answer quizzes (used by 85%). More effective or diverse formats like matching or fill-in-the-blank were rarely used.
Lethal mutations don't happen because teachers are careless. They happen when schools rush to adopt ideas without creating the conditions for deep understanding and professional dialogue.
